opus-5.5.text:
I think representation is really the foundation that generation sits on, even if for a long time the generative modeling community didn't treat it that way.

If you look at how diffusion models have developed, the dominant view was that the model learns everything end to end. You give it pixels, or latents from a VAE, and through denoising it somehow figures out both what the world looks like and how to render it. But when we actually probed these models, we found that the internal representations they learn are not that strong compared to what you get from self-supervised visual encoders like DINO. So the generative model is doing two jobs at once: it has to understand the structure of the visual world, the semantics, objects, how things relate, and it also has to produce fine-grained pixel detail. That's a very heavy burden.

That was a lot of the motivation behind work like REPA, representation alignment, where we simply align the intermediate features of the diffusion transformer with a pretrained visual representation. It's a very simple idea, but training converges much faster and quality improves. To me that's a signal that representation learning and generation aren't two separate fields. A good generative model is, implicitly, doing representation learning, and if you give it a good representation to lean on, it doesn't have to rediscover everything from scratch.

More broadly, I think the latent space matters enormously. Today most systems rely on a VAE whose latent space is optimized mainly for reconstruction, compressing and decompressing pixels. That isn't necessarily a semantically meaningful space. So a natural question is whether we can generate directly in a space shaped by strong representations, where the structure already reflects how we understand the visual world. Some of our more recent explorations, like using representation encoders as the basis for autoencoders, go in that direction.

For video it becomes even more important. Video isn't just a stack of pretty frames. It's about physics, causality, objects persisting over time. If you want a video model to become something like a world model, it needs an internal representation that captures how the world works, not just how it looks. I don't think you get that purely by scaling pixel reconstruction.

So my view is that representation is the "understanding" part, and generation is how that understanding gets expressed. In the long run I believe the two will converge into one system, where understanding and generation reinforce each other instead of being treated as different problems.

r001.rationale: The response calls representation the foundation of generation and says a good representation helps the model avoid rediscovering visual structure from scratch.

r002.rationale: The response says a world model needs an internal representation that captures how the world works, but it does not identify representation as the most important component of that world model.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually the central question, and it's one I've been obsessed with for a while.

For a long time, the generative modeling community and the representation learning community were sort of two different tribes. People doing self-supervised learning, contrastive learning, DINO, MAE, that kind of thing, cared about learning features that are good for understanding: classification, segmentation, retrieval. And the generative people, diffusion models, GANs, cared about pixel quality, FID scores, sample fidelity. The assumption was that if you want to understand images you learn representations, and if you want to generate images you learn a likelihood or a denoiser. Different objectives, different models.

My view is that this separation is artificial. To generate a realistic image or a coherent video, the model has to understand the world at some level. It has to know that a cup sits on a table and not float through it, that a dog has four legs, that when a person walks their legs alternate. All of that is semantic structure. A model that only memorizes pixel statistics will produce things that look locally plausible but globally wrong. So generation is implicitly a representation learning problem, whether you admit it or not.

What we found empirically, and this surprised a lot of people, is that diffusion models are actually not that good at learning representations on their own. If you probe the internal features of a standard diffusion transformer, they're much weaker than what you get from something like DINOv2. The model spends a huge amount of its capacity learning to reconstruct high-frequency details, noise patterns, textures, and comparatively little on semantics. And the training is slow partly because of that. It's trying to solve two problems at once, learning what the world looks like and learning how to render it, and it's doing the first one inefficiently.

That's the intuition behind REPA, representation alignment. The idea is very simple. You take a strong pretrained visual encoder, and you add a loss that encourages the intermediate features of the diffusion model to align with those semantic features. You're basically telling the generative model: don't rediscover semantics from scratch, here's a good representation, build on it. And the effect is dramatic. Training speeds up by more than an order of magnitude, and the final quality is better. That told us something important: the bottleneck in generation was never really the decoder, the rendering part. It was the representation.

The same thing shows up in the tokenizer, the VAE. People treated it as a compression tool, but the latent space it produces is the representation the diffusion model has to work in. If that latent space is unstructured, semantically meaningless, the diffusion model has to do all the hard work. If the latent space is already semantically organized, generation becomes much easier. So I've come to think of the tokenizer as a representation learner too, and we should design it that way rather than purely for reconstruction.

For video, the stakes go up. A video model needs some notion of physics, object permanence, causality over time. You can't fake that with texture statistics. So I think the path to good video generation runs directly through better representations of dynamics and 3D structure. In a sense, generation becomes the test of whether your representation actually captured the world, because the failures are visible. If the representation is missing something, the generated video will break in that exact place.

So the short version: representation is not a side effect of generation, it's the core of it. The longer term bet I'm making is that understanding and generation will converge into one system, where the same representation serves both, and each one makes the other better.

r001.rationale: The response says realistic generation requires the model to understand the world’s semantic structure and concludes that representation is central to generation.

r002.rationale: It connects world understanding to semantic structure, says better representations of dynamics and 3D structure are needed, and calls representation the core of generation.

astra-6.text:
I think representation is really at the center of this problem. Before asking how to generate an image or a video, you have to ask: in what space are we going to model it? Are we working directly with pixels, with compressed latent variables, or with something that captures objects and their relationships? That choice determines a lot of what the model can learn efficiently.

For recognition, a good representation often lets you ignore details. You want to recognize a dog regardless of the lighting or the texture of the background. But for generation, those details have to come back. So there’s a tension: you want a representation that captures the underlying structure, but you also need enough information to produce a rich, precise image.

With video, that becomes even more interesting. It’s not enough for each frame to look good. Objects have to persist, motion has to make sense, and the scene has to remain consistent over time. Ideally, the representation makes those relationships easier to learn, instead of forcing the model to rediscover them from an enormous sequence of pixels.

So I wouldn’t think of representation as just a compression step before generation. It shapes the learning problem itself. The question is how to find a space that makes generation both computationally manageable and capable of capturing the structure of the visual world.

r001.rationale: The response says representation is central to image and video generation and that the chosen space must support learning and capture visual structure.

r002.rationale: It describes representation as central to generation, but does not identify it as the most important component of a world model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think representation is one of the central questions in image and video generation. We often focus on the model—whether it’s a diffusion model or a transformer—but before that, there’s a more basic question: what space should the model operate in? Pixels? Compressed latent features? Something more semantic?

That choice determines what the model has to learn. In pixel space, it has to spend a lot of capacity modeling local details. With a useful latent representation, you can remove some of that redundancy and let the model focus more on structure and relationships. But compression also creates a bottleneck: if the representation discards something important, the generator has to reconstruct it, or it simply can’t recover it faithfully.

There’s also an interesting tension with recognition. For recognition, we often want invariance. We want to recognize the same object despite changes in lighting or viewpoint. For generation, those differences matter because you have to produce a particular image. So a representation that’s good for understanding isn’t automatically sufficient for generation.

For video, this becomes even more important. You need to represent not just how things look, but how they persist and change over time. Ideally, the representation makes objects, motion, and temporal relationships easier to model, rather than treating video as a collection of independent frames.

So I see representation and generation as deeply connected. A better representation can make the generative problem easier, and learning to generate can also help us discover what information a representation really captures.

r001.rationale: The response says a useful representation can make image and video generation easier by reducing redundancy and helping the model focus on structure and relationships.

r002.rationale: The response calls representation a central question, but does not mention a world model or identify representation as its most important component.
